summary: In this episode of Lord of Spirits, hosts Fr. Andrew Stephen Damick and Fr. Stephen De Young delve into the biblical and historical understanding of giants, also known as the Nephilim. They begin by examining Genesis 6:1-4, where the 'sons of God' take human wives, leading to the birth of the Nephilim. The hosts argue that the Nephilim are not the result of literal angel-human hybridization but rather the product of a ritual practice involving demonic spirits, human kings, and temple prostitutes, which was common in ancient Near Eastern cultures. This ritual, which they call the 'Nephilim ritual,' was a form of idolatrous sexual immorality that produced demonized human beings, often described as giants or tyrants. They support this interpretation with ancient texts, including the Book of Enoch and the Septuagint, and trace the theme of giants throughout the Old Testament, from the pre-flood world to the conquest of Canaan, where Israel was commanded to eradicate giant clans as an act of divine judgment.

entities.title: Og, King of Bashan
entities.summary: A giant king mentioned in the Bible, described as the last of the Rephaim. His bed was 15 feet long, indicating his great size. He was defeated by Israel under Moses, a victory commemorated in the Psalms.

entities.title: Goliath
entities.summary: A Philistine giant from Gath, described as a descendant of the Anakim. He was defeated by David, who acted as God's instrument. His bronze armor and height mark him as a remnant of the ancient giant clans.

entities.title: Septuagint
entities.summary: The Greek translation of the Hebrew Scriptures, produced in the 3rd century BC. It translates 'sons of God' as 'angels of God' and 'Nephilim' as 'giants,' showing the ancient Jewish understanding of Genesis 6.

entities.title: Book of Enoch
entities.summary: An ancient Jewish text, not in the canonical Bible, that expands on the story of the Watchers (fallen angels) and the Nephilim. It was influential in early Christianity and is quoted in the Epistle of Jude.

concepts.title: Nephilim Ritual
concepts.summary: The ritual practice involving a human king (or priest) embodying a demonic god and having sexual intercourse with a temple prostitute, resulting in offspring considered giants or Nephilim. This ritual was a form of idolatry and sexual immorality that produced demonized human beings.

concepts.title: Gigantomachy
concepts.summary: The war against giants, a recurring theme in the Old Testament where Israel, as God's instrument, fights against giant clans (e.g., the Amorites, Rephaim) who are demonically empowered and engaged in abominable practices.

concepts.title: Anti-Theosis
concepts.summary: The process by which a human being becomes like a demon through unrepentant sin and participation in demonic rituals, as opposed to theosis (becoming like God). Giants are examples of fully demonized humans.

concepts.title: Sethite Hypothesis
concepts.summary: A later interpretation, adopted by some Church Fathers (e.g., St. Augustine, St. John Chrysostom), that the 'sons of God' in Genesis 6 were descendants of Seth, not angels. This view arose in the late 4th century and became predominant, but the hosts argue it fails to account for the biblical and historical evidence.

claims.text: The Nephilim were not the result of literal angel-human hybridization, but were produced through a ritual involving a human king embodying a demon and a temple prostitute.
In the Bible, the term 'giant' does not primarily refer to physical size but to a demonically empowered tyrant or bully, as seen in the description of Goliath and other giant kings.
Jesus Christ, as the Son of David, continues the Gigantomachy by defeating demonic spirits through his ministry, exorcisms, and ultimately his death and resurrection.

scriptural_links.summary: The foundational passage about the sons of God, daughters of men, and the Nephilim. The hosts interpret this as describing the Nephilim ritual.
Mentions Og's bed of iron, which the hosts use as evidence of the Nephilim ritual and the size of giants.
Refers to Christ preaching to the spirits in prison who disobeyed in the days of Noah, which the hosts identify as the fallen angels of Genesis 6.
Mentions angels who did not keep their proper dwelling and gave themselves to sexual immorality, echoing the Genesis 6 narrative.

glossary.definition: The Hebrew word for giants, often translated as 'fallen ones' but more accurately meaning 'giants' or 'tyrants.' In the Bible, they are the offspring of the sons of God and daughters of men.
A group of giant kings, often associated with the underworld. Og of Bashan is described as the last of the Rephaim.
Angelic beings in the Book of Enoch who rebelled and taught forbidden knowledge to humanity, leading to the birth of the Nephilim.
